Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Avoid Religious Spaces: Places of worship or religious gatherings, Avoid Crowds: Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
  Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds

Vignette:
Elias was twenty-one when the convoy rolled into the valley, but the memory never settled into a straight line. It fractures now the way it did in the moment: a sudden impact that threw him against his harness, the sharp tang of burning insulation in the cabin air, and above it all, the relentless thrum of rotor blades cutting through dust. He knows what happened. He has lived it. Yet when anyone asks him to piece it together, his throat closes. The pieces refuse to align. He knows they are there—shards of sound, fragments of light—but he cannot find the words to hold them. Instead, they play over and over in his head, a film that starts without his permission, jolting awake long before his alarm goes off. After he came home, the world refused to feel safe. He caught himself scanning every doorway, every overpass, his eyes tracing the edges of rooms as if expecting the floor to give way. He had come to believe that danger was not an exception but the default state of things, that a single misstep could unravel everything. On his bus routes, he sits rigid behind the wheel, hands tight on the top of the steering column, listening to the idle rumble of the engine and the chatter of passengers. He is on guard all the time, counting exits, noting the spacing between vehicles, bracing for the next sudden noise. When a construction site down the avenue sends a dull crack through the streets, or when a passing aircraft thunders overhead, his breath catches. He knows he should be able to place the sound, to tell himself it is nothing, but his body does not wait for reason. He avoids religious spaces now. He stays away from the parish hall where his uncle leads weekly services, and he has stopped going to shopping centres and public events. The routes that wind through busy downtown stops are the ones he dreads, his stomach knotting as he waits for the next stop, knowing the doors will open and flood the aisle with strangers. Once, a street vendor’s cart caught fire a few blocks from his route, and the acrid scent of burnt insulation drifted into his open window. He pulled over immediately, killing the engine, his chest tightening until the moment passed. He sits alone in his apartment, the curtains drawn, knowing that staying still is the only way to keep from drowning. Elias spends long hours on his phone. He scrolls through games or watches videos until his eyes ache. The screen sits between him and the room, steady and predictable. The long hours have accumulated quietly. He has missed three shifts this month, calling in with vague excuses when the weight of the schedule finally breaks him. His dispatcher has stopped asking, and the foreman left a notice about his attendance. He sleeps poorly, wakes exhausted, and tells himself he will fix it tomorrow. He does not call his mother. He does not return texts from friends who used to check in. He sits on the edge of his bed, listening to the quiet house, and wonders how the days slipped through his fingers. What finally brought him through the door of the clinic was not a single breaking point, but a quiet exhaustion. He sat in the waiting room, his hands resting heavily on his knees, listening to the hum of the HVAC and the distant wail of a siren, and wondered if he would ever stop counting the ways things could go wrong. He is not sure his life is worth living anymore, not in the dramatic sense, but in the slow, heavy way that makes getting out of bed feel like a chore he no longer has the strength for. He does not know what he expects from the woman across from him. He only knows he cannot keep driving the same loop, and he wants, more than anything, to learn how to put the screen down without the dark coming back in.
